Clermont County Residents and Businesses Impacted by August Storms Eligible for Federal Disaster Assistance
Clermont and six other counties in Ohio counties have been approved for federal disaster assistance due to damage caused by severe weather in mid-August. The storms caused flooding, downed trees, multiple road closures and left thousands without power for days.
President Donald Trump approved Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine’s request for a “Major Disaster Declaration” for seven of 23 counties.
The declaration activates the Federal Emergency Management Agency’s (FEMA) Individual Assistance Grant Program, which includes grants for temporary housing and home repairs, rental assistance, replacement of personal property, crisis counseling, disaster unemployment assistance, and disaster legal services. The declaration also makes low-interest loans available through Small Business Administration (SBA).
Residents who sustained losses related to the severe weather in Clermont can begin applying for assistance at the federal government’s Disaster Assistance website or by calling 800-621-FEMA (3362). In addition, residents may be eligible for a valuation deduction for destroyed or damaged property. Visit the Auditor’s web site for information regarding the application process.
One-Time Homestead Property Tax Credit — House Bill 479
Ohio House Bill 479 provides a one-time, state-funded property tax credit to homeowners who qualify for the Homestead Exemption. The credit is expected to be approximately $450 to $500.
For real property, the credit will be applied automatically to tax year 2026 property tax bills issued in 2027. The credit for manufactured and mobile homes will apply to tax year 2027 bills.
Current Homestead recipients do not need to submit a separate application to receive this credit. However, homeowners who are not currently enrolled must apply for and qualify for the Homestead Exemption under the regular eligibility requirements described in the Homestead Program portion of the Auditor’s website .
The deadline is December 31, 2026; to be eligible for the one-time credit. Please be aware that there is no federal “Senior Homeowner Tax Review Request” form or federal program associated with this credit. For official information, contact the Clermont County Auditor’s Office at 513-732-7150 .
Current Property tax measures on the November 3rd Ballot
The following property-tax measures are currently listed by the Clermont County Board of Elections as approved for the November 3 ballot:
Batavia Township Fire and EMS — A new 8.4-mill continuing levy to provide and maintain a fire and emergency medical services department (Collection in calendar year 2028).
Bethel-Tate Local School District — Renewal of a 5.48-mill levy for five years to pay current operating expenses.
Clermont County Children Services — Renewal of a 0.8-mill levy for five years to support children services and the care and placement of children.
Union Township Safety Services — An additional 1.99-mill continuing levy to provide and maintain police, fire and emergency medical services.
U.S. Grant Joint Vocational School District — A 1.15-mill bond issue for 37 years, together with an additional 0.84-mill continuing tax levy, for general permanent improvements and payment of annual debt charges on the bonds.
Washington Township Police, Fire and EMS — An additional 5.5-mill levy for five years for police, fire and ambulance services.
The Clermont County Auditor’s Levy Calculator is now available online.
The Clermont County Auditor’s Levy Calculator is now available to help owners estimate the potential real estate tax impact of proposed property tax levies appearing on the November 3, 2026, General Election ballot. Property owners can access the calculator through the Auditor’s Property Search at clermontauditor.org . Users may search by owner name, property address or parcel number, select their property and view the estimated annual cost of the proposed levies applicable to that parcel.
IMPORTANT: Our Levy calculator estimates the cost of a proposed additional levy by applying the full voted millage rate to the property’s tax year 2025 value. The estimate does not include any first-year tax reduction factor that may subsequently be calculated and certified by the Ohio Department of Taxation under Ohio law. If the levy is approved, the actual amount charged may be different than the estimate shown. Final taxes will also depend on the property’s certified value, classification, eligibility for exemptions or credits, and all applicable state-certified tax rates and reduction factors. This calculator is provided for informational purposes only and is not intended to support or oppose any ballot issue.
Find Answers to Your Questions: Second-Half Property Tax Bills Delayed Due to HB 186 Tax Credits
Why are second-half property tax bills delayed?
Clermont County is implementing taxpayer credits required under Ohio House Bill 186 (HB 186). These calculations require software updates and detailed levy-specific adjustments to ensure taxpayers receive accurate tax relief.
What is HB 186?
HB 186 is an Ohio law designed to protect taxpayers from certain unintended property tax increases caused by rising property values and levy calculation mechanics.
Will my second-half bill be lower?
Potentially yes. Many taxpayers may receive a credit or reduction on their second-half property tax bill depending on their school district, applicable levies and valuation changes. School districts affected are Bethel-Tate; Blanchester; Clermont Northeastern; Felicity-Franklin; Goshen; Little Miami; West Clermont; Williamsburg and Great Oaks JVS.
Should I still pay my first-half taxes?
Yes. If you haven’t already done so, first-half tax payments remain unchanged and should be paid as normal.
Why is the County asking lenders to hold escrow payments?
If lenders automatically send estimated second-half payments before HB 186 credits are applied, taxpayers could overpay and later require refunds or escrow adjustments.
Will I be penalized if bills are delayed?
No. Updated due dates will be announced publicly, and taxpayers will have adequate time to make payment once bills are issued.
How will I know my updated amount due?
Updated second-half tax bills will reflect any HB 186 credits and will be mailed once calculations are finalized and made available on the Clermont County Auditor’s website
Who is Clermont County working with?
The County is coordinating with the following to ensure the accurate implementation of HB 186.
The Ohio Department of Taxation
Real Estate Software Vendors
Mortgage lenders and escrow companies
Local taxing authorities
State Associations
Where can I get updates?
Please monitor official communications from:
Clermont County Auditor’s Office
Clermont County Treasurer’s Office
or contact the offices directly with questions.
🔔Community Alert: Property Appraisers Across the County
Wondering why you’re seeing Clermont County Auditor vehicles or field appraisers in your neighborhood?
Our staff is currently out in the community collecting property data as part of our regular assessment process. The Clermont County Auditor’s Office is responsible for determining the value of every property in the county. This helps ensure fairness and accuracy in property taxation, as required by Ohio law.
🏡 What to expect:
➡️ Appraisers may visit properties that have experienced changes such as new construction, recent sales, damage, or demolition. ➡️ They are simply working to keep property records up to date and accurate. ➡️ Staff will be driving clearly marked Clermont County Auditor vehicles and carrying official identification. ➡️ If no one is available when they visit, they may leave a yellow door card with contact information and details about the visit.
Currently Passed Property Tax Reform – Fact Sheet
What Local Taxpayers Need to Know
Ohio enacted several property tax reform laws to reduce large, automatic tax increases caused by rising property values. Most changes take effect for Tax Year 2026 (bills paid in 2027), with some credits appearing as early as the second half tax bills for Tax Year 2025
Why This Matters in Clermont County
Clermont County experienced large valuation increases in recent years, which caused sharp jumps in property tax bills often without a new vote by taxpayers. These new laws are designed to slow those increases, add credits, and improve oversight.
Key Laws & What They Do
"> HB 124 – Property Valuation Process
What changed: Gives County auditors more authority in valuation decisions and clarifies appeal timelines.
What it means for you: Property values are still determined by the Clermont County Auditor, but the process is intended to be more transparent and predictable.
"> HB 129 – School “20-Mill Floor” Fix
What changed: More school levies are now counted toward the 20-mill floor.
Why it matters: This reduces automatic school-tax increases that used to occur simply because property values rose.
"> HB 186 – Inflation Cap & Tax Credits
What changed:
• Limits certain school-tax growth to inflation, not property value spikes
• Creates a new Inflation Cap Credit
• Gradually increases the Owner-Occupancy Credit
• Phases out the Non-Business Credit (agricultural land excluded)
What to look for on your bill: A new credit line reducing school taxes if your school district qualifies.
